paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 4, Laws of Motion: Newton's first law and inertia
paragraphs.key_phrase: mass is the measure of inertia
paragraphs.meaning: A body keeps its velocity unless a net external force acts, and how strongly it resists a change is its mass. One newton is defined as the force that gives a one kilogram mass an acceleration of one metre per second squared, so the first law is also a statement about what a force is. It further defines an inertial frame: the frames in which a force-free body really does travel in a straight line at constant speed.

words.meaning: The resistance of a body to any change in its state of rest or uniform motion.
words.breakdown: It is a property of mass. Doubling the mass doubles the force needed for the same acceleration.
words.trap: Inertia is not a force and does not push you backwards. In a braking bus your body continues at the old speed while the floor slows beneath you.

words.meaning: A frame in which a body with no net force has zero acceleration.
words.breakdown: A train at steady speed on straight track is close to one; a train braking into a station is not.
words.trap: The Earth is only approximately inertial because it rotates, which is why a Foucault pendulum slowly turns its plane. For a lab bench the approximation is good enough.

words.meaning: The vector sum of every force acting on a body from outside it.
words.breakdown: Forces between parts of the same body cancel in pairs, so they cannot change its overall motion.
words.trap: Constant velocity means zero net force, not zero forces. A tug of war at a standstill has large forces on both sides that cancel.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M20 112h280'/><rect class='d-line' x='70' y='64' width='70' height='40' rx='2'/><circle class='d-line' cx='88' cy='104' r='9'/><circle class='d-line' cx='124' cy='104' r='9'/><path class='d-accent' d='M160 84h44M192 76l12 8-12 8'/><text class='d-label' x='150' y='60'>net force</text><text class='d-label' x='70' y='136'>no net force, no change in velocity</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A cart on a line with the only force that changes its motion shown as a net force arrow.
paragraphs.hook: A book on a train table slides when the train brakes, and nothing pushed it.
paragraphs.exam_note: Statements about inertia and frames are usually a single-best-answer question, and the wrong option is the one that says a body at constant velocity has no forces on it.
paragraphs.trap: Zero net force is not zero force. A book resting on a table has its weight and the normal force in balance, and both are non-zero.

recall.q: A body moves with constant velocity. The net force on it is
recall.why: Constant velocity means no change in motion, so the vector sum of the forces is zero, even though individual forces act.
The larger the mass, the larger the force needed for a given acceleration, which is exactly what inertia means.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 4, Laws of Motion: Newton's second law and impulse
paragraphs.key_phrase: force is the rate of change of momentum
paragraphs.meaning: The second law is about momentum, not acceleration: force equals the rate at which momentum changes, and F = ma is the case where the mass stays constant. Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts, and it equals the change in momentum, which is why a fielder gives with the catch. A 0.16 kg cricket ball arriving at 30 m/s carries about 4.8 kg m/s, and stopping it in 0.01 s needs a force near 480 N.

words.meaning: The product of mass and velocity, a vector with units of kilogram metre per second.
words.breakdown: p = mv. A 0.16 kg ball at 30 m/s has 4.8 kg m/s.
words.trap: Momentum has direction, so a ball that rebounds has a larger change than one that stops. Ignoring the sign halves the answer.

words.meaning: The product of force and the time it acts, equal to the change in momentum.
words.breakdown: J = F Δt = Δp, and graphically it is the area under a force-time graph.
words.trap: Impulse is not a force and is not measured in newtons. Its unit is the newton second, the same as momentum.

words.meaning: The state in which all forces add to zero, so acceleration is zero.
words.breakdown: The body may be at rest or moving in a straight line at constant speed.
words.trap: Equilibrium does not mean at rest. A car at 80 km/h on a straight road is in equilibrium, and so is a book on a table.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 110h260M30 110V26'/><path class='d-fill' d='M60 110V60h40v50Z'/><path class='d-accent' d='M140 110V40h40v70Z'/><text class='d-label' x='56' y='50'>long time, small force</text><text class='d-label' x='136' y='32'>short time, large force</text><path class='d-guide' d='M100 96h40'/><text class='d-label' x='150' y='134'>equal areas, equal impulse</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Two force-time rectangles of equal area, one tall and narrow and one short and wide, showing the same impulse.
paragraphs.hook: A fielder who gives with the catch is buying time, and time is what turns a sting into a catch.
paragraphs.exam_note: Impulse questions usually give a force-time graph or a rebound and ask for the change in momentum, so read the area rather than the peak force.
paragraphs.trap: A ball hitting a wall and coming back at the same speed has a change of about 2mv, not mv, because the direction reverses.

recall.q: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 10 m/s and rebounds at 10 m/s. The magnitude of the impulse on it is
recall.why: Taking the incoming direction as positive, the change is m(-10) minus m(10), which is -4 kg m/s, so the magnitude is 4 N s.

recall.q: Pulling the hands back while catching a ball reduces
recall.why: The same momentum change takes longer, so the force is smaller. The impulse itself is fixed by the ball's momentum.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the impulse definition and units against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Ch 4, Laws of Motion: Newton's third law
paragraphs.key_phrase: action and reaction act on different bodies
paragraphs.meaning: Forces come in pairs of equal size and opposite direction, but the two members of a pair act on different bodies, so they never cancel. A 60 kg student standing in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s² feels a floor force of about 708 N, not 588 N, because the floor must both support the weight and supply the acceleration. A rocket works the same way in vacuum: it pushes exhaust backward and the exhaust pushes it forward.

words.meaning: Two forces of equal magnitude, opposite direction, acting on two different bodies.
words.breakdown: They arise together from one interaction and cannot be separated in time.
words.trap: Forces on the same body would cancel. Action and reaction never act on one body, which is why a horse can pull a cart.

words.meaning: The contact force a surface exerts perpendicular to itself.
words.breakdown: It is the reaction to the body pressing on the surface, and its size depends on the motion.
words.trap: The normal force is not always mg. In an upward-accelerating lift it exceeds the weight; at the top of a loop it can be less.

words.meaning: The total momentum of an isolated system stays constant.
words.breakdown: It follows from the third law, because internal forces cancel in pairs.
words.trap: Momentum is conserved only when no net external force acts. A ball bouncing off the ground is not an isolated system.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><rect class='d-line' x='40' y='50' width='60' height='60'/><path class='d-accent' d='M106 80h40M138 72l10 8-10 8'/><path class='d-muted' d='M34 80H6M14 72L4 80l10 8'/><text class='d-label' x='52' y='132'>wall pushes you left</text><text class='d-label' x='146' y='58'>you push the wall right</text><text class='d-label' x='150' y='104'>equal size, different bodies</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A hand pushing a wall to the right while the wall pushes the hand to the left, labelled as forces on different bodies.
paragraphs.hook: You cannot lift yourself by pulling your own hair, and the reason is that both forces act on you.
paragraphs.exam_note: The mark usually rests on the words different bodies, or on a lift question where the normal force is not equal to mg.
paragraphs.trap: Action and reaction are not cause and effect in time. They begin and end together, so calling one the cause of the other is wrong.

recall.q: Action and reaction forces never cancel because they
recall.why: Cancellation needs two forces on the same body. Each body of the pair feels only one of them.

recall.q: A 60 kg student stands in a lift accelerating upward at 2 m/s². The floor pushes up with about
recall.why: The net force must be ma, so the normal force is mg + ma, which is 588 + 120, about 708 N.

paragraphs.key_phrase: static friction adjusts, kinetic friction is fixed
paragraphs.meaning: Static friction is self-adjusting: it matches the applied force exactly until it reaches μsN, and only then does the box move. Kinetic friction then takes over at μkN, which is usually smaller, so starting a heavy almirah is harder than keeping it sliding. For dry wood on wood, μs is roughly 0.4 and μk about 0.3, and the standard model says neither depends on the area of contact.

words.meaning: The friction that holds a body at rest, matching the applied force up to a limit.
words.breakdown: f ≤ μsN. It is not fixed at μsN unless the body is on the point of moving.
words.trap: Writing static friction as μsN in every case fails whenever the push is smaller. It equals the push until the limit is reached.

words.meaning: The friction acting on a body that is already sliding, approximately μkN.
words.breakdown: It acts opposite to the relative motion and is nearly independent of speed.
words.trap: Doubling the sliding speed does not double the friction in this model. The coefficient does not depend on speed.

words.meaning: The steepest incline on which a body stays at rest.
words.breakdown: At that angle tan θ = μs, so the angle measures the static coefficient directly.
words.trap: The angle of repose uses μs, not μk. Using the kinetic value underestimates the steepest angle.

paragraphs.visual_alt: A block on a surface with an applied force arrow to the right and a friction arrow to the left.
paragraphs.hook: An almirah that will not budge does not need more strength, only one more newton than its static limit.
paragraphs.exam_note: Block-on-incline questions ask whether it slides at a given angle, and the answer is a comparison of tan θ with μs rather than with μk.
paragraphs.trap: Friction is not always μN. On a stationary block it equals the applied force, which may be far below the maximum.

recall.q: A block is pushed with 5 N on a floor where μsN is 12 N. The friction force is
recall.why: Static friction adjusts to the applied force, so it is 5 N here and only reaches 12 N when the push does.

recall.q: The angle of repose is the angle at which
options: The block just begins to slide
recall.why: At that angle the component of weight along the incline equals the maximum static friction, so sliding is about to begin.
